{{short description|American mathematical logician}}
'''Marian Boykan Pour-El''' (April 29, 1928 – June 10, 2009){{r|nams}} was an American [[mathematical logic]]ian who did pioneering work in [[computable analysis]].

==Early life and education==
Marian Boykan was born in 1928 in [[New York City]]; her parents were dentist Joseph Boykan and his wife Matilda (Mattie, née Caspe), a former laboratory technician and housewife.{{r|tribute|ias}}
As a young girl, she performed ballet at the [[Metropolitan Opera House (39th Street)|Metropolitan Opera House]],
and this influenced her later life where she was often more comfortable speaking before large audiences than in small groups.{{r|henrion}}
Although she wanted to attend the [[Bronx High School of Science]], it was at that time only for boys; instead, she went to a girls' school, [[Hunter College High School]].{{r|tribute}}

Her parents were unwilling to pay the tuition for private college for her, so she went to [[Hunter College]], an inexpensive local higher-education establishment primarily aimed at training schoolteachers.{{r|henrion}} There she earned a bachelor's degree in physics in 1949.{{r|tribute}} She also completed enough courses in mathematics for a second major but was not allowed to have two majors by Hunter College's rules.{{r|henrion}}

She was accepted to [[Harvard University]] for graduate studies in mathematics, with full support, as the only woman in the program.{{r|tribute}}
At Harvard, she earned a master's degree in 1951 and a Ph.D. in mathematical logic in 1958.{{r|utexas}} She was very isolated and lonely at Harvard, with few friends and, initially, no other students even willing to sit next to her in her classes.{{r|tribute|henrion}} The nearest restroom to her classes was in a different building, and one of the few buildings with air conditioning in the summers was off-limits to women, even when she was assigned as an instructor to a class in that building.{{r|henrion}} Because there were no logicians at Harvard at that time, she spent five years of her time as a visiting student at the [[University of California, Berkeley]].{{r|tribute|henrion|umn}} Her doctoral dissertation was ''Computable Functions''.{{r|mg}}

==Career==
After finishing her doctorate, Pour-El joined the mathematics faculty at [[Pennsylvania State University]].{{r|utexas}} She earned her tenure there in 1962.{{r|henrion}} During a sabbatical from 1962 to 1964 at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]], she worked with [[Kurt Gödel]].{{r|henrion|utexas|umn}}

She moved in 1964 to the [[University of Minnesota]], and was promoted to full professor there in 1968.{{r|tribute|umn}} Except for a year from 1969 to 1970 as a visiting professor at the [[University of Bristol]], she remained at the University of Minnesota until her retirement in 2000.{{r|utexas}}
At Minnesota, her doctoral students included [[Jill Zimmerman]] (Ph.D. 1990), later the James M. Beall Professor of Mathematics and Computer Science at [[Goucher College]], Maryland.{{r|zim}}

In 1980 Pour-El was elected as a Member at Large for the [[American Mathematical Society|AMS]] and served until 1982.<ref>{{Cite web |title=AMS Committees |url=http://www.ams.org/about-us/governance/committees/mal-past.html |access-date=2023-03-28 |website=American Mathematical Society |language=en |archive-date=2023-03-06 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230306081906/https://www.ams.org/about-us/governance/committees/mal-past.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Contributions==
Pour-El's early work concerned [[recursion theory]], and included joint work with{{r|tribute}} [[William Alvin Howard]],{{ran|H}} [[Saul Kripke]],{{ran|K}} [[Donald A. Martin]],{{ran|M}} and [[Hilary Putnam]].{{ran|P}}
In a 1974 publication, she studied analogues of computability for [[analog computer]]s. She proved that, for her formulation of this problem, the functions that can be computed by such computers are the same as the functions that define solutions to [[algebraic differential equation]]s.{{r|tribute}}{{ran|A}} This result, a refinement of the work of [[Claude Shannon]],
became known as the Shannon–Pour-El thesis.{{r|tribute}}

In the late 1970s Pour-El began working on [[computable analysis]].{{r|tribute}}
Her "most famous and surprising result",{{r|umn}} co-authored with Minnesota colleague J. Ian Richards, was that for certain computable [[initial condition]]s, determining the behavior of the [[wave equation]] is an [[undecidable problem]].{{r|tribute|umn}}{{ran|W}} Their result was later taken up by [[Roger Penrose]] in his book ''[[The Emperor's New Mind]]''; Penrose used this result as a test case for the [[Church–Turing thesis]], but concluded that the non-[[smooth function|smoothness]] of the initial conditions makes it implausible that a computational device could use this phenomenon to exceed the limits of conventional computing.{{r|tribute|penrose}} [[Freeman Dyson]] used the same result to argue for the evolutionary superiority of analog to digital forms of life.{{r|tribute|dyson}}

With Richards, Pour-El was the author of a book, ''[[Computability in Analysis and Physics]]''.{{r|tribute|utexas|umn|cap}}{{ran|C}}

==Recognition==
Pour-El was elected to the Hunter College Hall of Fame in 1975, and as a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] in 1983.
A symposium was held in honor of Pour-El in Japan in 1993.{{r|utexas}}

==Personal life==
As a student at Berkeley, Pour-El met her husband, Israeli biochemist [[Akiva Pour-El]].{{r|tribute|henrion|utexas|akiva}} They had one daughter, Ina. Her husband followed her to Penn State after completing his doctorate a year later,{{r|tribute|henrion}} and he later followed her, again, when she moved to Minnesota.{{r|henrion}} They lived separately for several long intervals, most notably from 1969 to 1975 when her husband taught in Illinois,{{r|tribute|henrion}} and Pour-El wrote an article in 1981 on how having a long-distance relationship worked for her.{{r|tribute}}{{ran|S}}

Pour-El's brother is music composer [[Martin Boykan]].{{r|brother}}
